images.next_text_full: How much did the model change? We want one number: 0 when nothing changed, larger when more changed. The standard answer is KL divergence, or KL, named after Solomon Kullback and Richard Leibler, who introduced it in 1951.

images.caption: Gains add to 0; every term is at least its gain, so the terms add to at least 0. A drop to 0.01 has log-ratio −3.689, but its term is only −0.037.
images.target_after_text: What about a huge drop? Take the vague answer from 0.40 down to 0.01, with the best answer rising to 0.51. The log-rati...
images.target_after_text_full: What about a huge drop? Take the vague answer from 0.40 down to 0.01, with the best answer rising to 0.51. The log-ratio of the vague answer is −3.689, a large negative number. But the weight is the new share, 0.01, so its term is only −0.037. A model that hardly says an answer gives that answer hardly any weight. The best answer's term is +0.738, and KL is 0.701.
images.next_text: You cannot get closer to a model than being the same model. KL starts at 0 for no change and only goes up.

images.caption: The two orders of KL: 0.047 and 0.042 for the small move; dropping an answer costs 0.102 one way and is infinite the other.
images.target_after_text: The swapped order appears in pretraining. The loss used there, cross-entropy, equals the entropy of the data plus KL(da...
images.target_after_text_full: The swapped order appears in pretraining. The loss used there, cross-entropy, equals the entropy of the data plus KL(data ‖ model). The entropy of the data does not depend on the model, so minimizing the loss minimizes that KL, with the data on top. The model has to give some probability to everything the data contains.
images.target_block_html: The swapped order appears in pretraining. The loss used there, cross-entropy, equals the entropy of the data plus KL(data ‖ model). The entropy of the data does not depend on the model, so minimizing the loss minimizes that KL, with the data on top. The model has to give some probability to everything the data contains.

images.caption: The new model writes replies, each drops its log-ratio, and the running average settles near 0.047. One simulated run.
images.target_after_text: Samples. KL is an average over the new model's replies, and averages can be estimated from samples. Let the new model w...
images.target_after_text_full: Samples. KL is an average over the new model's replies, and averages can be estimated from samples. Let the new model write replies, compute the log-ratio of each, and average. One simulated run on the egg example gives 0.096 after 10 replies, 0.061 after 100 and 0.048 after 10,000, against the exact 0.047. A single reply can have a negative log-ratio; the average settles on the positive value. The replies must come from the new model itself: lower the temperature or apply top-p, and the average no longer estimates this KL.
images.next_text: Tokens. A reply's probability is the product of its tokens' probabilities, each given the tokens before it. The log tur...
images.next_text_full: Tokens. A reply's probability is the product of its tokens' probabilities, each given the tokens before it. The log turns that product into a sum, so a reply's log-ratio is the sum of its tokens' log-ratios. Take a three-token reply with illustrative probabilities. The reference gives the tokens 0.40, 0.50 and 0.80, so the reply gets 0.16. The new model gives 0.50, 0.50 and 0.96, so the reply gets 0.24. The reply's log-ratio is log(1.5) = 0.405, and the tokens' log-ratios are 0.223, 0 and 0.182, which add up to 0.405.
images.target_block_html: Samples. KL is an average over the new model's replies, and averages can be estimated from samples. Let the new model write replies, compute the log-ratio of each, and average. One simulated run on the egg example gives 0.096 after 10 replies, 0.061 after 100 and 0.048 after 10,000, against the exact 0.047. A single reply can have a negative log-ratio; the average settles on the positive value. The replies must come from the new model itself: lower the temperature or apply top-p, and the average no longer estimates this KL.

images.caption: A reply's log-ratio splits over its tokens: 0.223 + 0 + 0.182 = 0.405, and the two places PPO and GRPO put it. Illustrative probabilities.
images.target_after_text: GRPO in DeepSeekMath adds the KL to the loss, with β = 0.04. Its per-token estimate, with x = π_ref / π, is x − log x −...
images.target_after_text_full: GRPO in DeepSeekMath adds the KL to the loss, with β = 0.04. Its per-token estimate, with x = π_ref / π, is x − log x − 1, which comes from the same straight-line fact and is never negative for any token.

images.caption: As KL grows, the reward keeps rising while gold peaks at 1.10 at KL 0.81 and falls. Toy example; each point is the best compromise at a smaller β.
images.target_after_text: KL 3.61: reward 2.67, gold −0.76, and the wrong answer now takes 69% of the replies.
images.target_after_text_full: KL 3.61: reward 2.67, gold −0.76, and the wrong answer now takes 69% of the replies.
images.next_text: The reward keeps rising the whole way, and the gold signal rises, peaks and falls. Gao, Schulman and Hilton reported th...
images.next_text_full: The reward keeps rising the whole way, and the gold signal rises, peaks and falls. Gao, Schulman and Hilton reported this pattern in 2022 for real reward models. The same paper warns that KL alone is a poor measure of how much over-optimization has happened. So KL is read next to the reward and the gold signal, and the checkpoint to keep is the one where gold peaks.
images.target_block_html: • KL 3.61: reward 2.67, gold −0.76, and the wrong answer now takes 69% of the replies.

images.caption: At the best compromise every log-ratio equals the reward minus 0.808. In a comparison the constant cancels: 0.731 either way.
images.target_after_text: That is the idea behind DPO, direct preference optimization. It skips the separate reward model: for each human-chosen...
images.target_after_text_full: That is the idea behind DPO, direct preference optimization. It skips the separate reward model: for each human-chosen pair, it uses β × log-ratio as the score and applies the same Bradley–Terry loss. On this pair the starting model has log-ratios of 0, a gap of 0 and a loss of 0.693. The best compromise has a gap of 1 and a loss of 0.313.
images.next_text: The log-ratio inside KL measures how far an answer moved, and it can also serve as that answer's reward.
